blocks.html: Every module in the lab is a model call with one extra idea around it.
The Concept First

HandsOnAI looks like many tools: chat, RAG, agents, workflows, loops, evaluation, vision and voice. Underneath, the shape is the same.

A model receives a payload and returns text. Everything else is a wrapper:

  • Chat adds a system prompt and a message list.
  • RAG searches documents and pastes the results into the prompt.
  • Agent gives the model tools and a loop.
  • Workflow organises stages as folders with review gates.
  • Loop repeats a step until a goal is met.
  • Evaluation asks a model to judge output against criteria.
  • Vision converts an image into tokens in the same request.
  • Voice converts speech to text and text to speech around the chat call.

The package is small on purpose. It is a learning lab, not a production framework. The goal is to make the concept visible, not to hide it.

That has a consequence for teaching: you do not need to cover every module. Teach the shape, then let the projects explore the wrappers.
Understanding Through a Food Truck

A food truck sells many dishes. The base is the same: a vehicle, a kitchen, a service window and a queue.

A new cuisine changes the ingredients and the menu, not the fact that someone cooks and someone serves.

HandsOnAI is the truck. The modules are the menu. The model call is the kitchen.
Discovering the Shape with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Map the Wrapper

Ask the AI to map each module to the call it wraps.

Here are the HandsOnAI modules:
[paste the list]

For each one, name what it adds around the model call. Include the new
input, the new state, the new loop or the new output. Mark any module
that is a side door rather than a stop on the main path.

A good answer will put vision and voice at the edges and the core loop through chat, RAG, agent, workflow and evaluation.

Exploration 2: Find the Shared Failure

Ask what can go wrong in every wrapper.

Every module ultimately calls a model. List the failures that can appear
in all of them, regardless of the wrapper. Include a fluent wrong answer,
a missing source, a tool error, a loop that will not stop and a cost
overrun.

The shared failures are the teaching opportunities.

Exploration 3: Choose the Depth

Ask what to skip.

A teacher has six hours for an introduction. The students can run
Python but have not built an AI system. Choose three modules to build
and two to demonstrate. Explain the sequence and what you would leave
out.

The answer is a curriculum decision, not a feature list.
From Concept to Practice

A module map:

Module Wrapper New input New risk
Chat System prompt and transcript Prompt history Hallucination, memory cost
RAG Search before the call Documents Stale index, unsupported citation
Agent Tools and a loop Tool results Tool misuse, runaway loop
Workflow Folders and review gates Stage outputs Vague stage contract
Loop Repetition and a goal Goal check Optimising the wrong measure
Evaluation A judge Criteria Bias, inconsistency
Vision Image tokens Image Miscounting, confident nonsense
Voice Speech converters Audio Noise, latency, turn-taking

The map is the course outline.
Build Task
Run the quickstart chat example. Then print the payload it sends. Mark which parts belong to the model and which belong to the wrapper.
Classroom Connection
Teach the shape before the modules. A student who can say "RAG is search plus a prompt" has a mental model that survives a change of framework.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 1.1 (Level 1). Name the wrapper that chat adds.

Exercise 1.2 (Level 2). Map three modules to their wrappers.

Exercise 1.3 (Level 3). Explain why the package is small on purpose.

Exercise 1.4 (Level 4). Choose three modules for a six-hour introduction and justify the choice.

Exercise 1.5 (Level 5). Design a one-hour lesson that teaches the shared shape without covering every module.
Chapter Summary

• Every module is a model call plus a wrapper.
  • The wrappers add prompts, evidence, tools, structure, repetition, judgement or senses.
  • The lab is small on purpose.
  • Teach the shape, then choose the modules.
  • Shared failures are teaching opportunities.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Mapped the wrappers
  • [ ] Named the shared failures
  • [ ] Chose a teaching depth
  • [ ] Ran one module
  • [ ] Identified what to skip
Your Learning Journal

1. Which wrapper was hardest to explain?
  2. Where does the model end and the wrapper begin?
  3. What would you teach first?
Next Steps
The shape is clear. The next chapter sets up a lab that can run it.
A classroom lab fails on setup before it fails on AI.
The Concept First

HandsOnAI needs Python 3.10+, the package and an OpenAI-compatible provider. There are three common setups:

  • Local Ollama: runs on the student machine or a lab machine. Private, offline-capable, limited by hardware.
  • Shared classroom server: one Ollama server on the network. Consistent, centralised, easier to monitor.
  • Cloud provider: an API key and a hosted model. Least setup, but data leaves the room and costs money.

The configuration is three environment variables:

export HANDS_ON_AI_SERVER="http://localhost:11434"
export HANDS_ON_AI_MODEL="llama3"
export HANDS_ON_AI_API_KEY=""

A local server needs no key. A hosted provider does. Never put a real key in a script, a slide or a repository.

The diagnostic command is:

handsonai doctor

Run it before class. It prints the server, model and key status, and checks the connection.
Understanding Through a Science Lab

A science lab is prepared before the students arrive: equipment, reagents, safety rules and a trial run.

If the equipment is missing, the lesson becomes a troubleshooting session. If the safety rules are unclear, the lesson becomes an incident.

A classroom AI lab needs the same preparation.
Discovering Setup with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Choose the Provider

Ask the AI to compare the options for a specific class.

A class of 25 students has old laptops, limited Wi-Fi and a strict
privacy policy. Compare local Ollama, a shared classroom server and a
cloud provider. Recommend one and name the trade-offs.

The answer should consider hardware, privacy, bandwidth, cost and support.

Exploration 2: Build the Checklist

Ask for a pre-class checklist.

Write a setup checklist for a HandsOnAI class. Include Python, the
package, the provider, the model, the diagnostic command, a test script,
the API key policy and a fallback if the network fails.

The fallback is part of the plan.

Exploration 3: Test the Failure

Ask what students see when the server is down.

The Ollama server is not running. Write the message a student should
see and the three checks they should make. Do not let the error look
like a model answer.

A setup failure should be diagnosable in minutes.
From Concept to Practice

A classroom setup checklist:

```markdown
Lab setup
Machines

• [ ] Python 3.10+
  • [ ] Package installed
  • [ ] Model available
  • [ ] handsonai doctor passes
Provider

• [ ] Local, shared or cloud
  • [ ] Server URL
  • [ ] Model name
  • [ ] Key policy
  • [ ] Cost limit
Classroom

• [ ] Test script
  • [ ] Offline fallback
  • [ ] Privacy and disclosure
  • [ ] Support contact ```
Build Task
Run the setup on one machine. Install the package, run handsonai doctor, run a chat call, and record the output. Then stop the server and record the failure.
Classroom Connection
A shared server reduces setup variance. A local model protects privacy. A cloud provider gives access to stronger models. The choice is a teaching and policy decision, not only a technical one.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 2.1 (Level 1). Name the three environment variables.

Exercise 2.2 (Level 2). Run handsonai doctor and record the result.

Exercise 2.3 (Level 3). Compare local, shared and cloud for a class of 25.

Exercise 2.4 (Level 4). Write the offline fallback for a network failure.

Exercise 2.5 (Level 5). Produce a complete classroom setup plan with a privacy and cost decision.
Chapter Summary

• The lab needs Python, the package and a provider.
  • Local, shared and cloud setups have different trade-offs.
  • Three environment variables configure the provider.
  • Run the doctor before class.
  • A fallback is part of the setup.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Chose a provider
  • [ ] Ran the doctor
  • [ ] Tested one call
  • [ ] Tested one failure
  • [ ] Wrote the fallback
Your Learning Journal

1. Which setup would you choose for your class?
  2. What failed first?
  3. What would you prepare before the students arrive?
Next Steps
The lab runs. The next chapter starts with chat, the module every other module wraps.
A chat model is stateless. The memory is a message list your code keeps.
The Concept First

A chat request has two kinds of message:

  • system: the standing instruction that sets role, tone and rules
  • user: the question or instruction for this turn

The model returns an assistant message. The next call starts fresh unless the application resends the earlier messages.

That is the whole mechanism behind "memory". A chat product stores the transcript and sends it again on each turn. More history means more tokens, more cost and a larger payload. The context window is the limit.

A bot is a function that calls the model with a fixed system prompt. A personality is a system prompt with a name.

Prompting improves when you are specific, provide context, show an example and define the output format.
Understanding Through a Conversation at a Counter

A clerk serves one customer at a time. When the next customer arrives, the clerk does not remember the previous conversation unless the notes are on the desk.

The transcript is the notes. The system prompt is the shop's policy card.
Discovering Chat with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Change the System Prompt

Ask the AI to compare two system prompts.

Here are two system prompts for the same question:
[paste them]

Explain what changes in the answer and what stays the same. Which
instruction is tone, which is constraint, and which is a claim the model
cannot verify?

A good answer will separate style from substance.

Exploration 2: Test the Memory

Ask what the model sees on the second turn.

A chat sends: system "You are a tutor", user "My name is Sam", assistant
reply, user "What is my name?". List the messages in the second request
and explain why the answer can use the name.

The model is not remembering. The code resent the transcript.

Exploration 3: Find the Cost

Ask what grows with the conversation.

A conversation has 20 turns. Explain what grows on each turn: tokens,
cost, latency and the risk of hitting the context window. Propose one
way to keep the conversation useful without resending everything.

Summarisation, retrieval and a shorter system prompt are all options.
From Concept to Practice

A chat record:

Field Entry
System prompt Tutor, one step at a time
User turn Explain a loop
Assistant reply Explanation and question
History Two messages
Tokens Usage from the call
Cache Enabled or not
Limit Context window and cost
Build Task
Run a Conversation with three turns. Print the message list before each call. Then set HANDS_ON_AI_CACHE and run the same prompt twice.
Classroom Connection
The stateless model is a core AI-literacy idea. A student who understands it can explain why a chat forgets, why a long conversation costs more and why a fresh chat behaves like a stranger.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 3.1 (Level 1). Explain the difference between the system and user messages.

Exercise 3.2 (Level 2). Run a three-turn conversation and print the history.

Exercise 3.3 (Level 3). Compare a system prompt that changes tone with one that adds a constraint.

Exercise 3.4 (Level 4). Measure the token growth over five turns.

Exercise 3.5 (Level 5). Design a memory strategy for a long classroom activity.
Chapter Summary

• Chat sends system and user messages and receives an assistant reply.
  • The model is stateless; memory is a resent transcript.
  • More history means more tokens and cost.
  • A bot is a function with a fixed system prompt.
  • Specific prompts and examples improve the answer.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Explained the stateless call
  • [ ] Printed a transcript
  • [ ] Compared two system prompts
  • [ ] Measured token growth
  • [ ] Chose a memory strategy
Your Learning Journal

1. What surprised you about memory?
  2. Which system prompt changed the answer most?
  3. When is a fresh chat the right choice?
Next Steps
Chat is the base. The next chapter adds evidence with RAG.

blocks.html: Retrieval-augmented generation is search plus a prompt with the results in it.
The Concept First

A model answers from two things: the prompt in front of it and what it learned during training. It does not know your notes, your policy or today's timetable.

RAG adds evidence:

  1. Index the documents: load, chunk, embed and save.
  2. Ask a question: embed the question, fetch the closest chunks, put them in the prompt, call the model.

The model still does the language work. The retriever does the finding. Both are needed.

The teaching points are the failure points:

  • a document that was never indexed is invisible
  • a stale index returns the old rule
  • a chunk boundary can cut an answer in half
  • a cited passage may not support the claim
  • the model may answer beyond the evidence
Understanding Through a Library Card Catalogue

A librarian does not reread every book when you ask a question. They use the catalogue to find a few passages, then read them with you.

The catalogue is the index. The passages are the context. The librarian's explanation is the model.
Discovering RAG with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Separate the Phases

Ask the AI to separate indexing from answering.

Here is a RAG description:
[paste it]

List the steps that happen once at indexing time and the steps that
happen on every question. Mark which steps cost a model call.

The separation prevents most confusion about RAG.

Exploration 2: Test the Evidence

Ask what a citation proves.

A RAG answer cites a document. Explain what the citation proves and what
it does not. Design a check that confirms the cited passage supports the
claim.

A citation label is not support. The passage is.

Exploration 3: Break the Index

Ask what happens when the source changes.

A policy changes, but the index is a week old. Explain what the bot
returns and how the class would detect the staleness. Propose a fix.

Re-indexing is a maintenance task, not a one-off setup step.
From Concept to Practice

A RAG record:

Field Entry
Documents Source, owner and date
Index Chunk size, embedding model, location
Question What the user asked
Retrieved Chunk IDs and scores
Answer The model response
Citation Document and passage
Check Does the passage support the claim?
Limitation Coverage and freshness
Build Task
Index a small folder of notes. Ask three questions: one answerable, one partly answerable and one not in the documents. Record the retrieved chunks and the answer for each.
Classroom Connection
RAG is the best module for teaching evidence. The student can see the source, the retrieved passage and the answer. The discussion is whether the passage actually supports the claim.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 4.1 (Level 1). Explain RAG in one sentence.

Exercise 4.2 (Level 2). List the indexing steps and the answering steps.

Exercise 4.3 (Level 3). Ask one answerable and one unanswerable question.

Exercise 4.4 (Level 4). Check whether a cited passage supports the answer.

Exercise 4.5 (Level 5). Design a small evaluation set for retrieval quality.
Chapter Summary

• RAG is search plus a prompt with evidence.
  • Indexing happens once; answering happens per question.
  • A citation is not proof; the passage is.
  • Stale indexes and chunk boundaries cause failures.
  • RAG is the best module for teaching evidence.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Separated indexing from answering
  • [ ] Asked an unanswerable question
  • [ ] Checked one citation
  • [ ] Found one limitation
  • [ ] Planned a re-index
Your Learning Journal

1. Which retrieved chunk was most useful?
  2. What did the bot answer without evidence?
  3. How would you keep the index fresh?
Next Steps
The answer has evidence. The next chapter gives the model tools.
A tool is a function the model may request. The harness decides whether it runs.
The Concept First

An agent adds two things to chat: tools and a loop.

A tool in HandsOnAI is a function with a simple contract:

  • a name
  • a description the model reads
  • one string input
  • one string output

The model proposes a tool call. The harness runs the function and adds the result to the transcript. The model reads the result and decides what to do next.

ReAct is the readable pattern: Thought, Action, Action Input, Observation, repeat, Final Answer.

The safety boundary is the tool list. A calculator is low risk. A file write, an email send or a payment is high risk. The model does not grant itself permission. The harness exposes the tools.
Understanding Through a Workshop

A craftsperson has a bench and a set of tools. The apprentice can ask for a tool, but the supervisor decides which tools are on the bench.

An agent is the apprentice. The tool list is the bench. The harness is the supervisor.
Discovering Agents with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Write the Tool Description

Ask the AI to turn a function into a tool description.

Here is a Python function:
[paste it]

Write the tool name, description and input format a model would need to
use it correctly. Include one example input and the error message for a
bad input.

The description is part of the interface.

Exploration 2: Trace the Loop

Ask for a step-by-step trace.

Here is an agent run:
[paste the trace]

Label each Thought, Action, Action Input, Observation and Final Answer.
Mark where the model changed its plan after an observation.

The trace is the lesson.

Exploration 3: Find the Dangerous Tool

Ask what should not be on the bench.

List the tools in this agent and classify each as read-only, write,
communicate or financial. Recommend which ones need a human approval
gate and what the gate should check.

A tool inventory is a risk assessment.
From Concept to Practice

A tool record:

Field Entry
Name calculator
Description Evaluate a Python arithmetic expression
Input Expression string
Output Result string
Risk Low
Gate None
Test 2 + 2 returns 4
Failure Bad input returns an error string
Build Task
Register one custom tool and run an agent that needs it. Print the trace. Then add a second tool and a question that needs both.
Classroom Connection
Agents teach decomposition, tool contracts and oversight. The visible trace is the assessment artefact: the student can explain why the agent chose a tool and where the result came from.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 5.1 (Level 1). Explain the tool contract.

Exercise 5.2 (Level 2). Write a description for a simple tool.

Exercise 5.3 (Level 3). Run an agent and label the trace.

Exercise 5.4 (Level 4). Classify three tools by risk and add one approval gate.

Exercise 5.5 (Level 5). Build a two-tool agent for a classroom task and document the failure modes.
Chapter Summary

• An agent adds tools and a loop.
  • A tool is a named function with a description and a string contract.
  • The model proposes; the harness runs.
  • The tool list is the safety boundary.
  • The trace is the teaching artefact.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Wrote a tool description
  • [ ] Ran an agent
  • [ ] Labeled the trace
  • [ ] Classified the tools
  • [ ] Added a gate
Your Learning Journal

1. Which tool description mattered most?
  2. Where did the model change its plan?
  3. Which tool would you never expose without approval?
Next Steps
The agent acts. The next chapter adds structure, repetition and judgement.
Structure is how a small model becomes a reliable process.
The Concept First

Three modules add control:

  • Workflow: numbered stage folders, each with instructions and an output. One stage runs at a time, and a person reviews before the next.
  • Loop: repeat a step until a goal is met. run_loop stops on a goal or a maximum number of iterations. run_ratchet keeps only improvements.
  • Evaluation: an LLM judge scores output against stated criteria.

They answer different questions:

  • Workflow: what are the stages, and where is the review gate?
  • Loop: when do we stop, and what counts as better?
  • Judge: how good is the output, against what standard?

A judge is a model producing a score. It can be biased, inconsistent and fooled by confidence. Calibrate it against human marks before trusting it.
Understanding Through a Production Line

A production line has stations, inspection benches and a stop rule. Each station does one job, and the inspector decides whether the work moves on.

A workflow is the line. A loop is the repetition. A judge is the inspector.
Discovering Control with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Design the Stages

Ask the AI to turn a task into a workflow.

Turn this task into a three-stage workflow:
[paste the task]

For each stage, write the instruction, the input, the output and the
review question. Explain what a person should check before the next
stage runs.

A stage without a review question is a black box.

Exploration 2: Define the Goal

Ask for a stopping rule.

A loop improves a paragraph until it is clear and under 100 words.
Write the goal check, the maximum iterations and the evidence that the
loop stopped for the right reason.

The goal is a test, not a feeling.

Exploration 3: Calibrate the Judge

Ask how to trust the score.

A judge scores 20 answers from 1 to 5. Design a calibration check
against your own marks. Include the agreement measure, the disagreements
you would read closely and the cases where the judge should not be used.

A judge is a signal, not a verdict.
From Concept to Practice

A control record:

Module Use Evidence
Workflow Research, outline, draft Stage outputs and review notes
Loop Improve until clear Goal check and iteration log
Ratchet Keep only improvements Score log and best version
Judge Score 20 answers Criteria, scores, human comparison
Build Task
Build a three-stage workflow with a review after each stage. Then build a loop with a goal check. Compare what each structure makes visible.
Classroom Connection
Structure is the difference between a demo and a process. Students can see the stage outputs, the loop log and the judge's reasoning. Those artefacts are easier to assess than a final paragraph.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 6.1 (Level 1). Explain the difference between a workflow and a loop.

Exercise 6.2 (Level 2). Write three stages for a writing task.

Exercise 6.3 (Level 3). Define a goal check and a maximum iteration count.

Exercise 6.4 (Level 4). Calibrate a judge against five human marks.

Exercise 6.5 (Level 5). Build a workflow with a judge at the review gate and document the failure modes.
Chapter Summary

• Workflows add stages and review gates.
  • Loops add repetition and a stopping rule.
  • Ratchets keep only improvements.
  • Judges score against criteria and need calibration.
  • Structure makes the process visible and assessable.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Designed a workflow
  • [ ] Defined a goal check
  • [ ] Ran a loop
  • [ ] Calibrated a judge
  • [ ] Named one failure mode
Your Learning Journal

1. Which structure made the work clearest?
  2. Where did the loop stop?
  3. When would you not trust the judge?
Next Steps
The process is structured. The next chapter adds senses.
Images and speech are input formats, not a new kind of intelligence.
The Concept First

A vision-language model converts an image into tokens and reads them alongside your text. describe("photo.jpg", "What is in this photo?") is the same call with one more input type.

A voice agent converts speech to text, calls the chat model, and converts the reply to speech. transcribe and speak are format converters.

The limitations are the lesson:

  • Vision miscounts, misses small text and gets spatial detail wrong.
  • A confident description can invent details.
  • Speech recognition struggles with noise and accents.
  • Voice latency adds up at every step.
  • Turn-taking and interruption are engineering problems, not model problems.
Understanding Through a Translator

A translator converts one language into another so the same conversation can happen. The translator does not make the speaker wiser.

Vision and voice are translators at the edges of the same conversation.
Discovering the Senses with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Test the Description

Ask the AI to compare a description with the image.

Here is an image description from a VLM:
[paste it]

List the claims that a person could verify from the image and the claims
that could be invented. Design three questions that would test the
model's counting, small-text reading and spatial accuracy.

The questions expose the limits.

Exploration 2: Design the Voice Loop

Ask for the simplest voice agent.

Design a voice loop using speech-to-text, chat and text-to-speech.
Include the recording step, the turn-taking rule, the latency budget and
the failure when the microphone is unavailable.

The hard part is around the model, not inside it.

Exploration 3: Find the Accessibility Use

Ask for a useful classroom application.

Design a vision or voice activity that improves accessibility rather
than replacing a student's work. Include the task, the check and the
privacy question.

Alt-text generation, spoken feedback and translation are candidates.
From Concept to Practice

A senses record:

Field Entry
Input Image or audio
Converter VLM, STT or TTS
Model Name and version
Output Text or audio
Check Counting, small text, noise or latency
Limitation What the model cannot see or hear
Privacy Where the file goes
Build Task
Describe one image and ask three questions: what is visible, how many objects, and what text is present. Compare the answers with the image. Then run a short speech-to-text test.
Classroom Connection
Vision and voice are engaging, which makes them good hooks. The lesson is the limitation: a fluent description is not a measurement, and a voice interface is not a conversation.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 7.1 (Level 1). Explain why vision is the same call with a new input.

Exercise 7.2 (Level 2). Describe an image and check one claim.

Exercise 7.3 (Level 3). Test counting, small text and spatial detail.

Exercise 7.4 (Level 4). Design a voice loop with turn-taking.

Exercise 7.5 (Level 5). Build an accessibility activity with a privacy and accuracy check.
Chapter Summary

• Vision and voice are input converters around the same call.
  • Vision is unreliable for counting, small text and spatial detail.
  • Voice adds latency, noise and turn-taking problems.
  • Engaging demos still need checks.
  • Accessibility is a strong use case.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Described one image
  • [ ] Tested three limitations
  • [ ] Designed a voice loop
  • [ ] Named a privacy question
  • [ ] Found an accessibility use
Your Learning Journal

1. Which vision claim was wrong?
  2. Where did voice latency appear?
  3. What would make the activity accessible?
Next Steps
The modules are mapped. The next chapter chooses a project.

blocks.html: The best project is the smallest one that teaches the thing you came to learn.
The Concept First

A project has a difficulty, a time, a module and a learning focus. Choosing well means matching those to the objective, not picking the most impressive demo.

A useful project brief states:

  • the learning objective
  • the module
  • the difficulty and time
  • the inputs and outputs
  • the check
  • the extension
  • the risk

The project gallery has more than forty options. Most are chat projects, which is useful: chat is the base every other module wraps.
Understanding Through a Recipe

A recipe tells you the dish, the time, the ingredients and the skill. You do not choose a wedding cake for a ten-minute lesson.

A project brief is a recipe for learning.
Discovering the Project with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Match Objective to Module

Ask the AI to choose from the objective.

My learning objective is: [paste it]
The time is: [90 minutes]
The students know: [Python basics]

Recommend a HandsOnAI module and project. Explain why it fits, what it
leaves out and what the student will be able to explain afterwards.

A good answer starts with the objective, not the project list.

Exploration 2: Cut the Scope

Ask what to remove.

Here is my project idea:
[paste it]

Cut it to the smallest version that still teaches the objective. Name
the features to defer and the one check that proves the core works.

The smallest version is the one that fits the lesson.

Exploration 3: Find the Risk

Ask what could go wrong.

The project uses a model, student data and a chat interface. List the
technical, privacy, cost and assessment risks. For each, name the
mitigation.

A project plan without risk is a demo plan.
From Concept to Practice

A project brief:

```markdown
Project: [name]
Objective: Module: Difficulty: Time: Inputs: Outputs: Core check: Extension: Risk: Evidence: ```
Build Task
Choose one project from the gallery. Write the brief. Cut it to the smallest version. Run the core check.
Classroom Connection
A project brief makes assessment easier. The student knows what "done" means, and the teacher can see whether the objective was met without judging polish.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 8.1 (Level 1). Name the four project attributes.

Exercise 8.2 (Level 2). Write a project brief for a chat activity.

Exercise 8.3 (Level 3). Cut a project to its smallest useful version.

Exercise 8.4 (Level 4). Name three risks and mitigations.

Exercise 8.5 (Level 5). Match three objectives to three projects and justify the choices.
Chapter Summary

• Match difficulty, time, module and focus to the objective.
  • Start with the objective, not the gallery.
  • Cut to the smallest version that teaches the thing.
  • Name the core check.
  • Plan the risk.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Wrote a project brief
  • [ ] Cut the scope
  • [ ] Named the core check
  • [ ] Named three risks
  • [ ] Chose the evidence
Your Learning Journal

1. Which project tempted you, and why?
  2. What did you cut?
  3. What is the smallest proof?
Next Steps
The project is chosen. The next chapter builds and reviews it.
A project is finished when someone else can run it and explain what it does.
The Concept First

A reliable project has six steps:

  1. Plan: the brief, the inputs and the check.
  2. Scaffold: the smallest runnable file.
  3. Implement: one feature at a time.
  4. Test: the core check and one failure.
  5. Document: run instructions, inputs, outputs and limits.
  6. Show: a short demo and an explanation.

The review is part of the build. A peer should be able to run the project, read the code and explain the model call.
Understanding Through a Workshop

A maker does not declare a chair finished because it looks like a chair. Someone sits on it. The joints are checked, the instructions are written and the next maker can reproduce it.

A project review is the sit test.
Discovering Review with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Plan the Scaffold

Ask for the smallest runnable version.

Here is the project brief:
[paste it]

Write the smallest runnable scaffold. It should run one prompt and print
the result. Name the next feature and the check for it.

A scaffold that does not run is not a scaffold.

Exploration 2: Review the Code

Ask for a review against the brief.

Here is the project code and brief:
[paste them]

Check the code against the brief. Does it meet the objective? Is the
model call visible? Are errors handled? Is the secret outside the code?
List the gaps in priority order.

The review is not a style opinion. It is a check against the brief.

Exploration 3: Test the Demo

Ask for a demo script.

Write a three-minute demo script for this project. Include the input,
the expected output, one failure and the explanation of the model call.

The demo is evidence of understanding.
From Concept to Practice

A review checklist:

  • [ ] The project runs from the README
  • [ ] The objective is visible
  • [ ] The model call is in one place
  • [ ] The secret is outside the code
  • [ ] One success and one failure are tested
  • [ ] The limitation is documented
  • [ ] The demo explains the idea
Build Task
Build the scaffold. Add one feature. Test the core check. Ask a peer to run it from the README without your help.
Classroom Connection
The review checklist is the assessment rubric. It rewards understanding, not polish. A small project that runs and explains itself is better than a large one that does not.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 9.1 (Level 1). List the six build steps.

Exercise 9.2 (Level 2). Write the smallest runnable scaffold.

Exercise 9.3 (Level 3). Test one success and one failure.

Exercise 9.4 (Level 4). Review a peer's project against the brief.

Exercise 9.5 (Level 5). Write the README and demo script for your project.
Chapter Summary

• Plan, scaffold, implement, test, document and show.
  • The review is part of the build.
  • A peer must be able to run and explain it.
  • Test one success and one failure.
  • The demo explains the model call.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Wrote the scaffold
  • [ ] Added one feature
  • [ ] Tested the core check
  • [ ] Wrote the README
  • [ ] Ran a peer review
Your Learning Journal

1. What broke first?
  2. What did the peer misunderstand?
  3. What would you cut next time?
Next Steps
The project works. The next chapter maps the gallery.
The gallery is a menu, not a checklist. Choose one project and finish it.
The Concept First

HandsOnAI ships projects across the modules:

  • Chat: personality bots, quizzes, journals, simulations, games, tutors, converters.
  • RAG: first RAG bot, QA CLI, PDF question answering, hybrid reasoning.
  • Agent: calculator, date tool, unit conversion, custom tool, multi-tool problem solving, evaluation.
  • Workflow: build a pipeline.
  • Loop: improve until good, build a Ralph loop.
  • Eval: judge your bot.
  • Vision: the talking picture.
  • Voice: the world's smallest Pipecat.

The projects share a template: difficulty, time, learning focus, module, overview, instructions, extensions and assessment.

The teaching risk is project sprawl. A student who starts five projects finishes none.
Understanding Through a Menu

A menu with forty dishes is not a meal. You choose one, eat it and decide what to try next.

The gallery is a menu. The lesson is the meal.
Discovering the Gallery with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Choose by Objective

Ask the AI to shortlist three projects.

Here is the learning objective and the time:
[paste them]

Shortlist three projects from the HandsOnAI gallery that fit. For each,
name the module, the core check and the reason it fits. Recommend one.

The objective filters the menu.

Exploration 2: Compare Difficulty

Ask what changes with difficulty.

Compare a beginner chat project with an intermediate agent project.
Explain the difference in code, concepts, time and assessment. Which
one teaches more per hour for a first course?

More difficulty is not more learning.

Exploration 3: Plan the Showcase

Ask how to present the project.

Design a five-minute showcase for a project. Include the objective, the
demo, one failure, the model call and the reflection. Do not let the
demo hide the limitation.

The showcase is an assessment opportunity.
From Concept to Practice

A gallery shortlist:

Project Module Time Core check Fit
Quiz bot Chat 45-60 min Score and feedback Lists, loops, parsing
First RAG bot RAG 45 min Answer cites a source Evidence
Calculator agent Agent 30-45 min Correct calculation via tool Tool contract
Improve until good Loop 45 min Goal check and log Iteration
Judge your bot Eval 45 min Score and human comparison Assessment
Build Task
Choose one project. Write the brief, the core check and the showcase plan. Do not start a second project until the first runs.
Classroom Connection
A completed small project is a better portfolio piece than five unfinished ones. The gallery supports choice; the brief creates focus.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 10.1 (Level 1). Name the project categories.

Exercise 10.2 (Level 2). Shortlist three projects for one objective.

Exercise 10.3 (Level 3). Compare two projects by learning per hour.

Exercise 10.4 (Level 4). Write a showcase plan with a failure.

Exercise 10.5 (Level 5). Build one project and map it to three learning objectives.
Chapter Summary

• The gallery covers chat, RAG, agents, workflows, loops, evaluation, vision and voice.
  • Projects share a template.
  • Choose by objective, not by novelty.
  • Finish one project before starting another.
  • The showcase is part of the assessment.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Shortlisted three projects
  • [ ] Chose one
  • [ ] Wrote the core check
  • [ ] Planned the showcase
  • [ ] Resisted the second project
Your Learning Journal

1. Which project fits your objective?
  2. What did you leave out?
  3. What will you show?
Next Steps
The project is chosen. The next chapter turns it into a lesson.

blocks.prompt: A student starts a quiz bot. By the second hour it has a database, a leaderboard, a login system and three unfinished modules. The core quiz does not run. The class ends in twenty minutes. Choose the next move.

options.label: Cut back to one quiz question, one score and one feedback message, then run the core check
options.outcome: The student finishes a small working project. The quiz asks a question, checks the answer and gives feedback. The extensions are listed as future work. The demo runs.
options.feedback: The best project is the smallest one that teaches the objective.

options.label: Push on and finish the login system before the demo
options.outcome: The login system takes the remaining time. The quiz still does not run, and the student cannot demonstrate the learning objective.
options.feedback: Finishing the wrong feature is not progress.

options.label: Demo the design and explain what it would do
options.outcome: The idea is clear and the code is not. The assessment cannot tell whether the student can build the model call or test the result.
options.feedback: A design is not a working project. Show one real check.

options.label: Start a simpler project from the gallery and abandon the quiz bot
options.outcome: The student starts again with twenty minutes left. The new project is also unfinished, and the first attempt is lost.
options.feedback: Cut the current project before replacing it.

blocks.debrief: Cut to the core check, run it, document the extension and show the model call. A finished small project beats an unfinished large one.

blocks.html: A lesson plan is a sequence of questions, not a tour of features.
The Concept First

HandsOnAI supports three teaching shapes:

  • Guided tour (1 hour): demonstrate the shape, run one module, discuss the limits.
  • Mini-project workshop (2-3 hours): plan, build, test and show one project.
  • Multi-week unit: chat, then RAG or agents, then a project and a showcase.

The lesson plan names:

  • the learning objective
  • the prior knowledge
  • the demonstration
  • the student task
  • the check
  • the discussion
  • the extension

A live demo can fail. That is a teaching opportunity if the failure is predictable and the fallback is ready.
Understanding Through a Cooking Class

A cooking class does not show forty recipes. It teaches one technique, demonstrates it, lets the students cook and tastes the result together.

The technique is the objective. The recipe is the project. The tasting is the assessment.
Discovering the Lesson with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Write the Objective

Ask the AI to start with what students will be able to explain.

Write a learning objective for a 90-minute HandsOnAI lesson. The students
know Python basics. The objective must be observable in a short demo or
explanation, not a vague appreciation of AI.

A good objective uses a verb: explain, build, test, compare.

Exploration 2: Plan the Flow

Ask for a timed sequence.

Turn this objective into a 90-minute lesson. Include the demonstration,
the student build, the check, the discussion and the buffer. Mark where
the model might fail and what the fallback is.

The buffer is part of the plan.

Exploration 3: Differentiate

Ask for three levels.

The class has beginners, students with some Python and a few advanced
students. Adapt the same project for each group without changing the
objective. Name the extension for the advanced group.

The objective stays; the scaffold changes.
From Concept to Practice

A 90-minute lesson:

Time Activity Evidence
10 Hook and objective Students can restate the goal
15 Demo one module Students see input and output
15 Plan the project Brief and core check
30 Build Running scaffold
10 Test and peer review One success and one failure
10 Showcase and discussion Explanation and limitation
Build Task
Write a 90-minute lesson for one project. Include the demo, the build, the check, the discussion and the fallback. Run the demo once before class.
Classroom Connection
The lesson is not the tool. The tool is the example. The objective, the check and the discussion are what the students take away.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 11.1 (Level 1). Name the three teaching shapes.

Exercise 11.2 (Level 2). Write one observable objective.

Exercise 11.3 (Level 3). Plan a 90-minute flow.

Exercise 11.4 (Level 4). Adapt the same project for three levels.

Exercise 11.5 (Level 5). Run the lesson and revise the timing from evidence.
Chapter Summary

• Teach a sequence of questions, not a feature tour.
  • Name the objective, task, check and discussion.
  • Use the 1-hour, workshop or multi-week shape.
  • Prepare a fallback for a demo failure.
  • Differentiate the scaffold, not the objective.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Wrote an observable objective
  • [ ] Planned the flow
  • [ ] Prepared the fallback
  • [ ] Adapted for three levels
  • [ ] Tested the demo
Your Learning Journal

1. Which part of the lesson took longest?
  2. Where did the demo fail?
  3. What did the students explain well?
Next Steps
The lesson runs. The final chapter assesses it and keeps it safe.

lessons.title: Assess, Disclose and Keep It Safe

blocks.html: Assessment should reward understanding, not the polished output of a model.
The Concept First

A HandsOnAI project can be assessed through:

  • Portfolio: the project, the code and the README.
  • Demonstration: a short run and an explanation.
  • Reflection: what the student learned about the model's limits.
  • Peer review: whether another student can run and explain it.
  • Test evidence: one success and one failure.

The assessment should make the model call visible. A student who cannot explain the call has not learned the module.

AI use also needs a policy:

  • Disclosure: when and how AI was used.
  • Privacy: what data may be sent to which provider.
  • Cost: who pays and what the limit is.
  • Accessibility: whether the tool works for every student.
  • Academic integrity: which tasks must be the student's own.
  • Safety: what the bot may not do.

A local model is easier to approve for sensitive material. A hosted model needs a contract and a data review.
Understanding Through a Driving Test

A driving test does not reward the smoothest passenger. It checks whether the driver can handle the car, the rules and an unexpected event.

A project assessment checks whether the student can run the project, explain the model call and handle a failure.
Discovering Assessment with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Build the Rubric

Ask the AI to turn the objective into a rubric.

Here is the project objective and the core check:
[paste them]

Write a four-level rubric for understanding, evidence, explanation and
responsible use. Do not reward polish over understanding.

A good rubric names what the student can explain.

Exploration 2: Write the Disclosure

Ask for a student-facing AI-use statement.

Write a short AI-use disclosure for a HandsOnAI project. Include which
tools were used, what they helped with, what was checked and what the
student wrote themselves.

Disclosure is a habit, not a punishment.

Exploration 3: Check the Data

Ask what leaves the room.

The project sends student text to a model. List the privacy, cost and
accessibility questions the instructor must answer before the lesson.
Include local versus hosted, retention and consent.

A classroom activity is a data-processing decision.
From Concept to Practice

An assessment record:

Element Evidence
Objective Brief and demo
Core check Test output
Explanation Student describes the model call
Failure One tested failure
Responsible use Disclosure and data policy
Reflection What the model cannot do
Build Task
Write the rubric, the disclosure statement and the data policy for your lesson. Ask one student or colleague to explain the model call without notes.
Classroom Connection
Assessment is the last chance to teach. The rubric tells students what matters: understanding, evidence and responsible use, not a fluent final answer.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 12.1 (Level 1). Name four assessment methods.

Exercise 12.2 (Level 2). Write a four-level rubric.

Exercise 12.3 (Level 3). Write an AI-use disclosure.

Exercise 12.4 (Level 4). Answer the privacy, cost and accessibility questions for your class.

Exercise 12.5 (Level 5). Run the assessment and compare the rubric with the student's explanation.
Chapter Summary

• Assess understanding, not polish.
  • Use a portfolio, demo, reflection, peer review and test evidence.
  • Disclose AI use.
  • Decide the data, cost and accessibility policy.
  • A local model is easier to approve for sensitive material.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Wrote the rubric
  • [ ] Wrote the disclosure
  • [ ] Answered the data questions
  • [ ] Checked accessibility
  • [ ] Ran the explanation check
Your Learning Journal

1. Which assessment caught the most understanding?
  2. What did the disclosure reveal?
  3. What data decision was hardest?
Next Steps
The course is assessed. The appendices collect the module map, the project template and the classroom checklist.
